text: Draw a line across the sky where space begins, and you get three different answers.
The group that keeps aviation records, the FAI, draws it at one hundred kilometres.
The US Air Force gave astronaut wings to anyone who flew higher than fifty miles. That's about eighty kilometres.
And in 2018, the astronomer Jonathan McDowell argued for eighty kilometres as well.
Now measure the famous record jumps against those lines. Felix Baumgartner, in 2012, began at almost thirty-nine kilometres.
Alan Eustace, in 2014, began at forty-one point four.
That is less than half of the hundred-kilometre line, and only about half of the eighty.
So the jumps from the so-called edge of space started in the stratosphere, which ends at about fifty kilometres.
They never reached any of the three lines.
So what is the edge, if no jump ever reached it? The full video on our channel has the answer. Like and subscribe so you don't miss the next one.
